section.heading: 5.6 Discrete Dynamical Systems
section.paragraph: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors provide the key to understanding the long-term behavior, or evolution, of a dynamical system described by a difference equation $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ . Such an equation was used to model population movement in Section 1.10, and will be used in various Markov chains in Section 5.9 and the spotted owl population in the introductory example for this chapter. The vectors $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ give information about the system as time (denoted by $$k$$ ) passes, where $$k$$ is a nonnegative integer. In the spotted owl example, for instance, $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ listed the numbers of owls in three age classes at time $$k$$ .

The applications in this section focus on ecological problems because they are easier to state and explain than, say, problems in physics or engineering. However, dynamical systems arise in many scientific fields. For instance, standard undergraduate courses in control systems discuss several aspects of dynamical systems. The modern state-space design method in such courses relies heavily on matrix algebra.1 The steady-state response of a control system is the engineering equivalent of what we call here the “long-term behavior” of the dynamical system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ .

Until Example 6, we assume that $$A$$ is diagonalizable, with $$n$$ linearly independent eigenvectors, $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}$$ , and corresponding eigenvalues, $$\text{λ} _{1},\ldots, \text{λ} _{n}$$ . For convenience, assume the eigenvectors are arranged so that $$| \text{λ} _{1}| \geq | \text{λ} _{2}| \geq \cdots \geq | \text{λ} _{n}|$$ . Since $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ is a basis for $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , any initial vector $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ can be written uniquely as
$$\textbf{x}_{0} = c_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \textbf{v}_{n}$$

This eigenvector decomposition of $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ determines what happens to the sequence $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ . The next calculation generalizes the simple case examined in Example 5 of Section 5.2. Since the $$\textbf{v}_{i}$$ are eigenvectors,
$$\textbf{x}_{1} = A \textbf{x}_{0} & = c_{1} A \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} A \textbf{v}_{n} & = c_{1} \lambda_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \lambda_{n} \textbf{v}_{n}$$
and

$$\textbf{x}_{2} & = A \textbf{x}_{1} = c_{1} \lambda_{1} A \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \lambda_{n} A \textbf{v}_{n} & = c_{1} \left(\right. \lambda_{1} \left.\right)^{2} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \left(\right. \lambda_{n} \left.\right)^{2} \textbf{v}_{n}$$
In general,

$$\textbf{x}_{k} = c_{1} \left(\right. \lambda_{1} \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{1} + \hdots + c_{n} \left(\right. \lambda_{n} \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{n} \left(\right. k = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots \left.\right)$$
The examples that follow illustrate what can happen in (2) as $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ .
section.heading: A Predator–Prey System
section.paragraph: Deep in the redwood forests of California, dusky-footed wood rats provide up to $$80\%$$ of the diet for the spotted owl, the main predator of the wood rat. Example 1 uses a linear dynamical system to model the physical system of the owls and the rats. (Admittedly, the model is unrealistic in several respects, but it can provide a starting point for the study of more complicated nonlinear models used by environmental scientists.)

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Denote the owl and wood rat populations at time $$k$$ by $$\textbf{x}_{k} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} O_{k} \\ R_{k} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , where $$k$$ is the time in months, $$O_{k}$$ is the number of owls in the region studied, and $$R_{k}$$ is the number of rats (measured in thousands). Suppose
$$\begin{matrix}O_{k + 1} & = \left(\right. .5 \left.\right) O_{k} + \left(\right. .4 \left.\right) R_{k} \\ R_{k + 1} & = - p \cdot O_{k} + \left(\right. 1.1 \left.\right) R_{k}\end{matrix}$$

where $$p$$ is a positive parameter to be specified. The $$(.5)O_{k}$$ in the first equation says that with no wood rats for food, only half of the owls will survive each month, while the $$(1.1)R_{k}$$ in the second equation says that with no owls as predators, the rat population will grow by $$10\%$$ per month. If rats are plentiful, the $$(.4)R_{k}$$ will tend to make the owl population rise, while the negative term $$- p \cdot O_{k}$$ measures the deaths of rats due to predation by owls. (In fact, $$1000p$$ is the average number of rats eaten by one owl in one month.) Determine the evolution of this system when the predation parameter $$p$$ is $$.104$$ .

image.alt: A figure shows a spotted owl on a tree branch and a dusky-footed wood rat underneath with a bidirectional arrow in between them.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: When $$p = .104$$ , the eigenvalues of the coefficient matrix $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} .5 & .4 \\ {- p} & 1.1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ for the equations in (3) turn out to be $$\text{λ} _{1} = 1.02$$ and $$\text{λ} _{2} = .58$$ . Corresponding eigenvectors are
$$\textbf{v}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} , \textbf{v}_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$
An initial $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ can be written as $$\textbf{x}_{0} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . Then, for $$k \geq 0$$ ,

$$\textbf{x}_{k} & = c_{1} \left(\right. 1.02 \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \left(\right. .58 \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{2} & = c_{1} \left(\right. 1.02 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}10 \\ 13\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} + c_{2} \left(\right. .58 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}5 \\ 1\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

As $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ , $$(.58)^{k}$$ rapidly approaches zero. Assume $$c_{1} > 0$$ . Then, for all sufficiently large $$k$$ , $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ is approximately the same as $$c_{1}(1.02)^{k}\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , and we write
$$\textbf{x}_{k} \approx c_{1} \left(\right. 1.02 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix}$$
The approximation in (4) improves as $$k$$ increases, and so for large $$k$$ ,

$$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} \approx c_{1} \left(\right. 1.02 \left.\right)^{k + 1} \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} = \left(\right. 1.02 \left.\right) c_{1} \left(\right. 1.02 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 13 \end{bmatrix} \approx 1.02 \textbf{x}_{k}$$

The approximation in (5) says that eventually both entries of $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ (the numbers of owls and rats) grow by a factor of almost $$1.02$$ each month, a $$2\%$$ monthly growth rate. By (4), $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ is approximately a multiple of $$(10,13)$$ , so the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ are nearly in the same ratio as $$10$$ to $$13$$ . That is, for every $$10$$ owls there are about $$13$$ thousand rats.

section.paragraph: Example 1 illustrates two general facts about a dynamical system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ in which $$A$$ is $$n \times n$$ , its eigenvalues satisfy $$| \text{λ} _{1}| \geq 1$$ and $$1 > | \text{λ} _{j}|$$ for $$j = 2,\ldots,n$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ . If $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is given by equation (1), with $$c_{1} \neq 0$$ , then for all sufficiently large $$k$$ ,
$$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} \approx \lambda_{1} \textbf{x}_{k}$$
and
$$\textbf{x}_{k} \approx c_{1} \left(\right. \lambda_{1} \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{1}$$

The approximations in (6) and (7) can be made as close as desired by taking $$k$$ sufficiently large. By (6), the $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ eventually grow almost by a factor of $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ each time, so $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ determines the eventual growth rate of the system. Also, by (7), the ratio of any two entries in $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ (for large $$k$$ ) is nearly the same as the ratio of the corresponding entries in $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ . The case in which $$\text{λ} _{1} = 1$$ is illustrated in Example 5 in Section 5.2.
section.heading: Graphical Description of Solutions
section.paragraph: When $$A$$ is $$2 \times 2$$ , algebraic calculations can be supplemented by a geometric description of a system’s evolution. We can view the equation $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ as a description of what happens to an initial point $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ as it is transformed repeatedly by the mapping $$\textbf{x}\mapsto A\textbf{x}$$ . The graph of $$\textbf{x}_{0},\textbf{x}_{1},\ldots$$ is called a trajectory of the dynamical system.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Plot several trajectories of the dynamical system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ , when
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} .80 & 0 \\ 0 & . 64 \end{bmatrix}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The eigenvalues of $$A$$ are $$.8$$ and $$.64$$ , with eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . If $$\textbf{x}_{0} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , then
$$\textbf{x}_{k} = c_{1} ( .8 )) k \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_{2} \left(( .64 )\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Of course, $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ tends to $$\textbf{0}$$ because $$(.8)^{k}$$ and $$(.64)^{k}$$ both approach $$0$$ as $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ . But the way $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ goes toward $$0$$ is interesting. Figure 1 shows the first few terms of several trajectories that begin at points on the boundary of the box with corners at $$( \pm 3, \pm 3)$$ . The points on each trajectory are connected by a thin curve, to make the trajectory easier to see.

image.alt: A graph shows the origin as an attractor with several lines and curves pointing towards the origin. Many points are marked on the lines and curves.

figure.caption: Figure 1 The origin as an attractor

section.paragraph: In Example 2, the origin is called an attractor of the dynamical system because all trajectories tend toward $$\textbf{0}$$ . This occurs whenever both eigenvalues are less than 1 in magnitude. The direction of greatest attraction is along the line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and the eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ for the eigenvalue of smaller magnitude.

In the next example, both eigenvalues of $$A$$ are larger than $$1$$ in magnitude, and 0 is called a repeller of the dynamical system. All solutions of $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ except the (constant) zero solution are unbounded and tend away from the origin.2

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Plot several typical solutions of the equation $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ , where
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1.44 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.2 \end{bmatrix}$$
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The eigenvalues of $$A$$ are $$1.44$$ and $$1.2$$ . If $$\textbf{x}_{0} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then
$$\textbf{x}_{k} = c_{1} \left(\right. 1.44 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_{2} \left(\right. 1.2 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Both terms grow in size, but the first term grows faster. So the direction of greatest repulsion is the line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and the eigenvector for the eigenvalue of larger magnitude. Figure 2 shows several trajectories that begin at points quite close to $$\textbf{0}$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows the origin as a repeller with various lines and curves pointing away from the origin. Many points trace the lines and the curves.

figure.caption: Figure 2 The origin as a repeller

section.paragraph: In the next example, $$\textbf{0}$$ is called a saddle point because the origin attracts solutions from some directions and repels them in other directions. This occurs whenever one eigenvalue is greater than $$1$$ in magnitude and the other is less than $$1$$ in magnitude. The direction of greatest attraction is determined by an eigenvector for the eigenvalue of smaller magnitude. The direction of greatest repulsion is determined by an eigenvector for the eigenvalue of greater magnitude.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Plot several typical solutions of the equation $$\textbf{y}_{k + 1} = D\textbf{y}_{k}$$ , where
$$D = \begin{bmatrix} 2.0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}$$

(We write $$D$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ here instead of $$A$$ and $$\textbf{x}$$ because this example will be used later.) Show that a solution $$\{\textbf{y}_{k}\}$$ is unbounded if its initial point is not on the $$x_{2} \text{-axis}$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The eigenvalues of $$D$$ are $$2$$ and $$.5$$ . If $$\textbf{y}_{0} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then
$$\textbf{y}_{k} = c_{1} 2^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + c_{2} \left(\right. .5 \left.\right)^{k} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

If $$\textbf{y}_{0}$$ is on the $$x_{2} \text{-axis}$$ , then $$c_{1} = 0$$ and $$\textbf{y}_{k}\rightarrow\textbf{0}$$ as $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ . But if $$\textbf{y}_{0}$$ is not on the $$x_{2} \text{-axis}$$ , then the first term in the sum for $$\textbf{y}_{k}$$ becomes arbitrarily large, and so $$\{\textbf{y}_{k}\}$$ is unbounded. Figure 3 shows ten trajectories that begin near or on the $$x_{2} \text{-axis}$$ .

image.alt: A graph shows the origin as a saddle point with four straight lines and several curves in the form of a plus sign. Many points trace the lines and the curves.

figure.caption: Figure 3 The origin as a saddle point

section.heading: Change of Variable
section.paragraph: The preceding three examples involved diagonal matrices. To handle the nondiagonal case, we return for a moment to the $$n \times n$$ case in which eigenvectors of $$A$$ form a basis $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ for $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ . Let $$P = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} \textbf{v}_{1} & \cdots & \textbf{v}_{n} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and let $$D$$ be the diagonal matrix with the corresponding eigenvalues on the diagonal. Given a sequence $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ satisfying $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ , define a new sequence $$\{\textbf{y}_{k}\}$$ by
$$\textbf{y}_{k} = P^{- 1} \textbf{x}_{k} , \text{or equivalently} , \textbf{x}_{k} = P \textbf{y}_{k}$$
Substituting these relations into the equation $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ and using the fact that $$A =$$ $$PDP^{- 1}$$ , we find that
$$P \textbf{y}_{k + 1} = A P \textbf{y}_{k} = \left(\right. P D P^{- 1} \left.\right) P \textbf{y}_{k} = P D \textbf{y}_{k}$$
Left-multiplying both sides by $$P^{- 1}$$ , we obtain
$$\textbf{y}_{k + 1} = D \textbf{y}_{k}$$
If we write $$\textbf{y}_{k}$$ as $$\textbf{y}(k)$$ and denote the entries in $$\textbf{y}(k)$$ by $$y_{1}(k),\ldots,y_{n}(k)$$ , then

$$\begin{bmatrix} y_{1} \left(\right. k + 1 \left.\right) \\ y_{2} \left(\right. k + 1 \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ y_{n} \left(\right. k + 1 \left.\right) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \lambda_{1} & 0 & \hdots & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_{2} & & \vdots \\ \vdots & & \ddots & 0 \\ 0 & \hdots & 0 & \lambda_{n} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} y_{1} \left(\right. k \left.\right) \\ y_{2} \left(\right. k \left.\right) \\ \vdots \\ y_{n} \left(\right. k \left.\right) \end{bmatrix}$$

The change of variable from $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ to $$\textbf{y}_{k}$$ has decoupled the system of difference equations. The evolution of $$y_{1}(k)$$ , for example, is unaffected by what happens to $$y_{2}(k),\ldots,y_{n}(k)$$ , because $$y_{1}(k + 1) = \text{λ} _{1} \cdot y_{1}(k)$$ for each $$k$$ .

The equation $$\textbf{x}_{k} = P\textbf{y}_{k}$$ says that $$\textbf{y}_{k}$$ is the coordinate vector of $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ with respect to the eigenvector basis $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{n}\}$$ . We can decouple the system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ by making calculations in the new eigenvector coordinate system. When $$n = 2$$ , this amounts to using graph paper with axes in the directions of the two eigenvectors.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Show that the origin is a saddle point for solutions of $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ , where
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1.25 & - . 75 \\ - .75 & 1.25 \end{bmatrix}$$
Find the directions of greatest attraction and greatest repulsion.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Using standard techniques, we find that $$A$$ has eigenvalues $$2$$ and $$.5$$ , with corresponding eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , respectively. Since $$|2| > 1$$ and $$|.5| < 1$$ , the origin is a saddle point of the dynamical system. If $$\textbf{x}_{0} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , then
$$\textbf{x}_{k} = c_{1} 2^{k} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \left(\right. .5 \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{2}$$
This equation looks just like equation (8) in Example 4, with $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ in place of the standard basis.

On graph paper, draw axes through $$\textbf{0}$$ and the eigenvectors $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ . See Figure 4. Movement along these axes corresponds to movement along the standard axes in Figure 3. In Figure 4, the direction of greatest repulsion is the line through $$\textbf{0}$$ and the eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ whose eigenvalue is greater than $$1$$ in magnitude. If $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is on this line, the $$c_{2}$$ in (9) is zero and $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ moves quickly away from $$\textbf{0}$$ . The direction of greatest attraction is determined by the eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ whose eigenvalue is less than $$1$$ in magnitude.

image.alt: A graph shows the origin as a saddle point with four straight lines and eight curves in the form of a cross sign. Points are marked on the lines and curves tracing them.

figure.caption: Figure 4 The origin as a saddle point

example.paragraph: A number of trajectories are shown in Figure 4. When this graph is viewed in terms of the eigenvector axes, the picture “looks” essentially the same as the picture in Figure 3.

section.heading: Complex Eigenvalues
section.paragraph: When a real $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$A$$ has complex eigenvalues, $$A$$ is not diagonalizable (when acting on $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ ), but the dynamical system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ is easy to describe. Example 3 of Section 5.5 illustrated the case in which the eigenvalues have absolute value $$1$$ . The iterates of a point $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ spiral around the origin along an elliptical trajectory.

If $$A$$ has two complex eigenvalues whose absolute value is greater than $$1$$ , then $$\textbf{0}$$ is a repeller and iterates of $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ will spiral outward around the origin. If the absolute values of the complex eigenvalues are less than $$1$$ , then the origin is an attractor and the iterates of $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ spiral inward toward the origin, as in the following example.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: It can be verified that the matrix
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} .8 & .5 \\ - .1 & 1 .0 \end{bmatrix}$$

has eigenvalues $$.9 \pm .2i$$ , with eigenvectors $$\begin{bmatrix} {1 \mp 2i} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Figure 5 shows three trajectories of the system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ , with initial vectors $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ 2.5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 3 \\ 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 0 \\ {- 2.5} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .

image.alt: A figure shows three dotted curves traced by points from the origin spiraling towards the axis. The size of points is increasing.

figure.caption: Figure 5 Rotation associated with complex eigenvalues

section.heading: Survival of the Spotted Owls
section.paragraph: Recall from this chapter’s introductory example that the spotted owl population in the Willow Creek area of California was modeled by a dynamical system $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ in which the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{k} = (j_{k},s_{k},a_{k})$$ listed the numbers of females (at time $$k$$ ) in the juvenile, subadult, and adult life stages, respectively, and $$A$$ is the stage-matrix

MATLAB shows that the eigenvalues of $$A$$ are approximately $$\text{λ} _{1} = .98$$ , $$\text{λ} _{2} = - .02 + .21i$$ , and $$\text{λ} _{3} = - .02 - .21i$$ . Observe that all three eigenvalues are less than 1 in magnitude, because $$| \text{λ} _{2}|^{2} = | \text{λ} _{3}|^{2} = ( - .02)^{2} + (.21)^{2} = .0445$$ .

For the moment, let $$A$$ act on the complex vector space $$\textbf{\mathbb{C}}^{3}$$ . Then, because $$A$$ has three distinct eigenvalues, the three corresponding eigenvectors are linearly independent and form a basis for $$\textbf{\mathbb{C}}^{3}$$ . Denote the eigenvectors by $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ . Then the general solution of $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ (using vectors in $$\textbf{\mathbb{C}}^{3}$$ ) has the form

$$\textbf{x}_{k} = c_{1} \left(\right. \lambda_{1} \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \left(\right. \lambda_{2} \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3} \left(\right. \lambda_{3} \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{3}$$

If $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is a real initial vector, then $$\textbf{x}_{1} = A\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is real because $$A$$ is real. Similarly, the equation $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = A\textbf{x}_{k}$$ shows that each $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ on the left side of (11) is real, even though it is expressed as a sum of complex vectors. However, each term on the right side of (11) is approaching the zero vector, because the eigenvalues are all less than $$1$$ in magnitude. Therefore the real sequence $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ approaches the zero vector, too. Sadly, this model predicts that the spotted owls will eventually all perish.

Is there hope for the spotted owl? Recall from the introductory example that the $$\text{18} \%$$ entry in the matrix $$A$$ in (10) comes from the fact that although $$\text{60} \%$$ of the juvenile owls live long enough to leave the nest and search for new home territories, only $$\text{30} \%$$ of that group survive the search and find new home ranges. Search survival is strongly influenced by the number of clear-cut areas in the forest, which make the search more difficult and dangerous.

Some owl populations live in areas with few or no clear-cut areas. It may be that a larger percentage of the juvenile owls there survive and find new home ranges. Of course, the problem of the spotted owl is more complex than we have described, but the final example provides a happy ending to the story.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Suppose the search survival rate of the juvenile owls is $$\text{50} \%$$ , so the $$(2,1) \text{-entry}$$ in the stage-matrix $$A$$ in $$(10)$$ is $$.3$$ instead of $$.18$$ . What does the stage-matrix model predict about this spotted owl population?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Now the eigenvalues of $$A$$ turn out to be approximately $$\text{λ} _{1} = 1.01$$ , $$\text{λ} _{2} = - .03 + .26i$$ , and $$\text{λ} _{3} = - .03 - .26i$$ . An eigenvector for $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ is approximately $$\textbf{v}_{1} =$$ $$(10,3,31)$$ . Let $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{3}$$ be (complex) eigenvectors for $$\text{λ} _{2}$$ and $$\text{λ} _{3}$$ . In this case, equation (11) becomes

$$\textbf{x}_{k} = c_{1} \left(\right. 1.01 \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2} \left(\right. - .03 + .26 i \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{2} + c_{3} \left(\right. - .03 - .26 i \left.\right)^{k} \textbf{v}_{3}$$

As $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ , the second two vectors tend to zero. So $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ becomes more and more like the (real) vector $$c_{1}(1.01)^{k}\textbf{v}_{1}$$ . The approximations in equations (6) and (7), following Example 1, apply here. Also, it can be shown that the constant $$c_{1}$$ in the initial decomposition of $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is positive when the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ are nonnegative. Thus the owl population will grow slowly, with a long-term growth rate of $$1.01$$ . The eigenvector $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ describes the eventual distribution of the owls by life stages: for every $$31$$ adults, there will be about $$10$$ juveniles and $$3$$ subadults.

section.paragraph: 1 See G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell, and A. Emami-Naeimi, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, 5th ed. (Upper Saddle River, NJ: Prentice-Hall, 2006). This undergraduate text has a nice introduction to dynamic models (Chapter 2). State-space design is covered in Chapters 7 and 8.

2 The origin is the only possible attractor or repeller in a linear dynamical system, but there can be multiple attractors and repellers in a more general dynamical system for which the mapping $$\textbf{x}_{k}\mapsto\textbf{x}_{k + 1}$$ is not linear. In such a system, attractors and repellers are defined in terms of the eigenvalues of a special matrix (with variable entries) called the Jacobian matrix of the system.
